records.name: Causation Tracking
records.definition: Recording which event caused which, so cause-and-effect chains can be reconstructed later.

records.name: Correct Workflow Reasoning
records.definition: The ability to reason correctly about a workflow's steps by knowing their causal relationships.

records.name: Unordered Side Effects
records.definition: Applying side effects in an order that ignores their causal dependencies, producing incorrect outcomes.

records.name: Arbitrary Reordering

distinctFrom.reason: Arbitrary reordering lets any effect appear before its cause, while a read-your-writes violation is one writer reading back a stale copy of its own write.

records.definition: Reordering causally related operations freely, so effects can appear before their causes.

records.name: Causal Ordering
records.definition: The requirement that operations be applied in an order consistent with their cause-and-effect relationships.

records.name: Eventual Consistency Safety
records.definition: The degree to which replicas can converge over time without ever exposing a causally impossible state.

records.name: Latency/Availability
records.definition: The degree to which enforcing causal ordering across replicas costs added latency and reduced availability.

records.name: User-Visible Ordering Guarantees
records.definition: The ability to guarantee that users never observe an effect before its cause.

records.name: Causal Reasoning
records.definition: Reasoning about which events must precede others based on their causal relationships.

records.name: Ordering Semantics
records.definition: The requirement that a defined semantics specify when one event is considered to happen before another.

records.name: Parallel Execution
records.definition: The degree to which enforcing a happens-before order constrains how much work can run in parallel.

records.name: Race Detection
records.definition: The ability to detect data races by finding accesses with no happens-before ordering between them.

records.name: Correct Stateful Processing
records.definition: The ability to process a stream statefully with correct results by handling events in their proper order.

records.name: Ordering Key or Sequence
records.definition: The requirement that each event carry a key or sequence number that fixes its position in order.

records.name: Unordered Parallel Consumption
records.definition: Consuming an ordered event stream in parallel without preserving order, so state is updated out of sequence.

records.name: Dependency Declaration
records.definition: The requirement that each operation declare the operations it causally depends on.

records.name: Graph Complexity
records.definition: The degree to which tracking fine-grained causal dependencies grows the dependency graph large and hard to reason about.

records.name: Hidden Dependency

distinctFrom.reason: A hidden dependency is an undeclared requirement of a component or an operation, while test pyramid inversion is a suite weighted toward slow end-to-end tests.

records.definition: A dependency a component or an operation relies on without declaring it, so it surfaces only at runtime or when an unstated order is broken.

records.name: Cycle Detection
records.definition: The ability to detect cycles in a dependency graph before they cause deadlock or infinite resolution.

records.name: Dependency Extraction
records.definition: The requirement that dependencies between units be discovered and represented explicitly as a graph.

records.name: Dynamic Loading
records.definition: The degree to which resolving dependencies dynamically at runtime undermines a statically analyzable dependency graph.

records.name: Bidirectional Collaboration
records.definition: The degree to which forbidding cycles prevents two components from depending on each other bidirectionally.

records.name: Build Order
records.definition: The ability to derive a correct build or execution order from a graph that contains no cycles.

records.name: Layering
records.definition: A convention of organizing components into ordered layers where each may depend only on the layers beneath it.

records.name: Topological Ordering
records.definition: The ability to linearize a directed acyclic graph into an order where every node follows its dependencies.

records.name: Concurrent Update Detection
records.definition: The ability to detect when two updates happened concurrently rather than one causally after the other.

records.name: Metadata Size
records.definition: The degree to which carrying a per-node counter for every node grows the ordering metadata with cluster size.

records.name: Node Identity
records.definition: The requirement that each participating node have a distinct identity to index its own counter.

records.name: Single Global Clock Assumption
records.definition: Assuming a single global clock orders all events, which fails across distributed nodes with independent clocks.

records.name: Version Vector
records.definition: A set of per-node counters that together capture the causal history of a replicated item.

records.name: Happens-Before Reasoning
records.definition: Reasoning about event order using logical timestamps that respect the happens-before relation.

records.name: Logical Counter
records.definition: A monotonically increasing counter each process maintains to stamp events for logical ordering.

records.name: No Concurrent Causality Distinction
records.definition: The degree to which a single logical counter cannot tell concurrent events apart from causally ordered ones.

records.name: Partial Ordering
records.definition: The ability to establish a consistent partial order over events without a shared physical clock.

records.name: Wall-Clock Ordering Assumption
records.definition: Ordering distributed events by wall-clock timestamps, which clock skew makes unreliable.

records.name: Clock Skew
records.definition: The degree to which physical clocks on different nodes drift apart, distorting time-based ordering.

records.name: Physical-Clock-Only Ordering
records.definition: Ordering events by physical clocks alone, which clock skew renders inconsistent across nodes.

records.name: Wall-Clock-Correlated Causal Order
records.definition: The ability to order events causally while keeping timestamps close to wall-clock time.

records.name: Commutative Merge
records.definition: The requirement that concurrent updates merge in any order to the same result.

records.name: Conflict-Free Replica Convergence
records.definition: The ability for replicas to converge to one state automatically without conflict resolution.

records.name: Last-Write-Wins Overwrite
records.definition: Resolving concurrent updates by keeping the most recent write, rather than merging all updates.

records.name: Metadata Overhead
records.definition: The degree to which the bookkeeping a conflict-free type carries per value adds storage and transmission cost.

records.name: Identical Delivery Order Across Nodes
records.definition: The ability to deliver messages to every node in the same total order.

records.name: Per-Node Independent Ordering
records.definition: Letting each node decide message order independently, so replicas diverge on sequence.

records.name: Assumed Total Consistency And Availability
records.definition: Assuming a distributed system can be fully consistent and available at once, ignoring partitions that force a choice.

records.name: Explicit Consistency/Availability Choice Under Partition
records.definition: The ability to choose deliberately between consistency and availability when a network partition occurs.

records.name: Network Partition Possibility
records.definition: The requirement that a distributed design account for the possibility of network partitions.

records.name: Consistency Assumed Free When Healthy
records.definition: Assuming consistency carries no cost while the network is healthy, ignoring the latency it still imposes.

records.name: Latency-Consistency Trade-off When Healthy
records.definition: The ability to weigh the latency-versus-consistency trade-off that remains even when the network is healthy.

records.name: Reorder Buffer
records.definition: A technique for holding events that arrive early until the events before them arrive, then releasing them in order.
